name: Be technically and tactically proficient
definition: Before you can lead, you must be able to do the job; the first principle is to know your job. As a Marine, you must demonstrate your ability to accomplish the mission and be capable of answering questions and demonstrating competence in your military occupational specialty (MOS).

rows.situation: When you are asked to lead work you do not yet know
rows.under: Takes the title and hopes the people who know it will carry you.
rows.justRight: Learns the job well enough to do it, answer questions, and judge the work.
rows.over: Refuses to lead until you are the best expert in the room.

rows.situation: When someone asks how the work is actually done
rows.under: Points at a specialist and cannot say the next step yourself.
rows.justRight: Answers from the work, or says what you still need to learn and goes to learn it.
rows.over: Gives a lecture that buries the one thing they needed to do today.

rows.situation: When the job has moved past what you already know
rows.under: Stays on last year's method and calls it experience.
rows.justRight: Spends time with people who are current, and practices the new piece until you can do it.
rows.over: Keeps practicing the new piece after you can already do it, and this week's work waits.

rows.situation: When the next job up is already in view
rows.under: Waits to be taught it after the promotion.
rows.justRight: Learns the duties of the next seat now, so you can take them without a scramble.
rows.over: Studies the next seat so hard that this week's job slips.

rows.situation: When the tools or the method have changed
rows.under: Keeps using the old way because you already know it.
rows.justRight: Learns the new way well enough to teach it, and drops the old way when it no longer serves.
rows.over: Chases every new tool and the team never settles.
